title: The collector and the settings that send to it

story: The telemetry collector works. It is the service that receives the usage numbers Claude Code sends (cost, tokens, sessions), and it deletes prompts and emails before anything is stored. Now it runs on inf, our internal Kubernetes cluster, and the first week of numbers looks wrong. The frontend team's cost on the dashboard is about half of what the Anthropic invoice says. The reason is boring. Half the team works from home without the VPN, so their Claude Code tries to send its numbers to an internal address it cannot reach, and quietly drops them. The machines of Nova, our ticket-to-PR agent, are worse off: they live in a separate AWS account with no route to inf at all, so not a single agent number has arrived.

The obvious fix is to put the collector on the internet. But then anyone who finds the address can write to it, and a script could send a million fake cost points to the spend dashboard you show leadership. And even with the right address, 25 engineers would each have to type the same eight settings correctly, and keep them correct for months.
hook.question: How do we let every laptop and every agent send to one public address, without letting strangers write to it, and without asking each person to set it up?

read.h: A public door that only accepts writes with a key
p: Three things are involved: the senders (Claude Code on a laptop, or inside an agent's VM), the door (a public address, otel.rhinohealth.com), and the collector behind it. The door is deliberately narrow. Our public entry point, the proxy that receives all traffic from the internet, passes only two paths, /v1/metrics and /v1/logs, which are the two paths OTLP (the OpenTelemetry protocol) uses for metrics and events over HTTP. A web application firewall, or WAF, sits in front and inspects each request for attack patterns. If the WAF itself breaks, requests are refused instead of let through unchecked, which people call failing closed.

The real lock is inside the collector. Every request must carry an ingest token in its Authorization header, the same Bearer header you know from calling any API. The collector checks it with an extension called bearertokenauth. A request without the header, or with the wrong token, gets 401 before any processor runs, so nothing from a stranger reaches the database.

This token can only write telemetry. It cannot read a dashboard, query a database or call anything else. That matters, because the token will sit on every laptop, and something that sits on 25 laptops will leak one day. If it leaks, the worst anyone can do is write junk, and we change the token in one place.

code.file: collector.yaml (the part that checks the token)
code.text:
extensions:
  bearertokenauth:
    token: ${env:INGEST_TOKEN}

receivers:
  otlp:
    protocols:
      http:
        endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4318
        auth:
          authenticator: bearertokenauth

service:
  extensions: [bearertokenauth]

notes.text: The collector reads the token from an environment variable when it starts, so the file itself holds no secret and can live in git. On inf, a Kubernetes secret filled from Vault provides the variable.
The receiver hands every request to the extension first. Only requests with the right token continue into the pipeline.
Defining an extension is not enough: it must also be switched on here. Forget this line and the collector refuses to start, which is the safe way to fail.

p: Now the senders. Claude Code already speaks OpenTelemetry; it needs a few environment variables to know that it should send, what to send and where. If each person sets them by hand, some will forget, some will copy an old address, and some will enable prompt logging to debug something and forget to disable it. The numbers then describe whoever happened to set it up right, not the team.

So the variables arrive through managed settings, the settings file that an organisation pushes to every Claude Code and that a person cannot override. We keep the file in git, next to the other managed settings, so every change is reviewed. The file turns telemetry on, sends metrics and events as OTLP over HTTP to otel.rhinohealth.com, and turns every content flag off, so prompts, answers and tool details never leave the laptop. The collector still deletes them again, because a rule that depends on every laptop being right is not a rule.

One value is different: the ingest token. The file in git says only "<set only in the admin console>" where the token goes, and the real token is typed only into the admin console of claude.ai, which sends the settings to every laptop. A token in git would be a token in every clone of the repo, forever, even after we change it.

notes.text: The main switch. Without it, nothing else in this block does anything.
Only the base address. The exporter adds /v1/metrics and /v1/logs itself, which are exactly the two paths the door lets through.
Standard OpenTelemetry format: name=value pairs. The exporter turns it into the header Authorization: Bearer <token> on every request.
Content flags off at the source. The real file switches off two more of them, for assistant answers and tool content.
Resource attributes are labels attached to everything this process sends. Every person gets the same two, so there is no team here: the file is the same for the whole company.

deeper.h: Go deeper: why these are environment variables
p: None of these names belong to Claude Code. OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT, OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS and OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES are defined by the OpenTelemetry specification, and every OpenTelemetry SDK reads them, in Node, Python or Go. That is why a later lesson can tag an agent's numbers by setting one of these variables per session, without changing a line of the agent's code.

read.h: A person becomes a team at the door
p: Claude Code puts the person's work email on every number it sends, so the dashboards could show cost per person. We do not want that: numbers about one person turn a tool for the team into a tool for watching people. So the collector, which already deletes content, also turns each email into a team name and then deletes the email.

The table of work email to team lives in Vault, and it changes when people join or move. When we deploy the collector, Terraform reads the table and writes one line per person into the collector's configuration. Next to the team, the collector keeps a salted hash of the email: the email is mixed with a secret value (the salt) and turned into a long string that cannot be turned back into the email. It lets us count how many different people used Claude this week, without being able to say who they were.

code.file: collector.yaml (what the deploy writes from the team table)
code.text:
processors:
  transform/people:
    error_mode: ignore
    metric_statements:
      - context: datapoint
        statements:
          - set(attributes["team"], "frontend") where attributes["user.email"] == "sean@rhinohealth.com"
          - set(attributes["team"], "backend") where attributes["user.email"] == "dana@rhinohealth.com"
          - set(attributes["user.hash"], SHA256(Concat([attributes["user.email"], "${env:USER_SALT}"], ""))) where attributes["user.email"] != nil
          - delete_key(attributes, "user.email")

notes.text: A metric arrives as data points, one per combination of labels. The statements run on each data point. Events get the same list with context: log.
One line per person, written by the deploy from the table in Vault. The real table has every engineer in it.
The salt comes from the environment, like the token, so the file in git holds no secret.
After this line, no record carries a name.

deeper.h: Go deeper: the agents hold no ingest token
p: An agent's VM reads text that anyone can write, so it holds no long-lived secret, and the ingest token is no exception. The plan is a small relay inside the LLM gateway, the service that already checks each run's short-lived run token for model calls. The VM sends its telemetry to the relay with that run token, the relay checks it and forwards to the collector with the real ingest token. The VM's copy of the settings therefore has no token and no team; the harness, our program that runs Claude Code in the VM, adds the run's own labels to each session.

lab.title: A collector that only takes writes with a key
lab.goal: Run a collector that refuses every request without the ingest token, and that turns each person's email into a team before anything leaves it.

guess.q: The collector's configuration defines bearertokenauth and uses it in the receiver, but someone forgot to list it under service.extensions. What happens when you start the collector?

options.text: It starts and accepts every request, because the check is not switched on.
options.why: That would be the dangerous way to fail. The receiver needs an authenticator it cannot find, so the collector does not start at all.

options.text: It refuses to start, and says it cannot find the authenticator.
options.why: The receiver asks for bearertokenauth, which was never started. The collector stops with 'authenticator not found', so you notice at once instead of running an open door.

options.text: It starts, and every request gets 401, even with the right token.
options.why: The collector checks its whole configuration before it opens the port. A missing extension is caught at start, not per request.

follow.say: Make a folder for the lab and write the collector configuration from Understand, with both parts: the token check and the team table. The debug exporter prints every record instead of storing it, so you can read what would reach the database.
follow.do:
mkdir -p ~/academy-labs/g1-1 && cd ~/academy-labs/g1-1 && cat > collector.yaml <<'EOF'
extensions:
  bearertokenauth:
    token: ${env:INGEST_TOKEN}

receivers:
  otlp:
    protocols:
      http:
        endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4318
        auth:
          authenticator: bearertokenauth

processors:
  transform/people:
    error_mode: ignore
    metric_statements:
      - context: datapoint
        statements:
          - set(attributes["team"], "frontend") where attributes["user.email"] == "sean@rhinohealth.com"
          - set(attributes["team"], "backend") where attributes["user.email"] == "dana@rhinohealth.com"
          - set(attributes["user.hash"], SHA256(Concat([attributes["user.email"], "${env:USER_SALT}"], ""))) where attributes["user.email"] != nil
          - delete_key(attributes, "user.email")

exporters:
  debug:
    verbosity: detailed

service:
  extensions: [bearertokenauth]
  pipelines:
    metrics:
      receivers: [otlp]
      processors: [transform/people]
      exporters: [debug]
EOF

follow.say: Write one cost number the way Claude Code sends it: the metric claude_code.cost.usage, 42 cents, with the model and the person's email as labels.
Start the collector. The token and the salt arrive as environment variables, the same way the Kubernetes secret delivers them on inf.
follow.do: docker run -d --name otel-door -p 4318:4318 -e INGEST_TOKEN=lab-ingest-token -e USER_SALT=lab-salt -v "$PWD/collector.yaml:/etc/otelcol-contrib/config.yaml" otel/opentelemetry-collector-contrib:0.161.0 && sleep 4 && docker logs otel-door 2>&1 | tail -1 | cut -c1-100
follow.see:
7924d83e2546…
2026-10-15T23:34:01.893Z	info	service@v0.161.0/service.go:256	Everything is ready. Begin r

follow.say: Be the stranger first: send the number with no token, and then with a wrong one.
follow.do:
curl -s -w ' -> %{http_code}\n' -X POST http://localhost:4318/v1/metrics -H 'Content-Type: application/json' --data @cost.json
curl -s -w ' -> %{http_code}\n' -X POST http://localhost:4318/v1/metrics -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -H 'Authorization: Bearer wrong-token' --data @cost.json
follow.see:
{"code":16, "message":"missing or empty authorization header: Authorization"} -> 401
{"code":16, "message":"provided authorization does not match expected scheme or token"} -> 401

follow.say: Now send it like a laptop with the managed settings: the same header that OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS produces.
follow.do: curl -s -w ' -> %{http_code}\n' -X POST http://localhost:4318/v1/metrics -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -H 'Authorization: Bearer lab-ingest-token' --data @cost.json

follow.say: Read what would reach the database. Look for the email: it should be gone, with a team and a hash in its place.
follow.do: sleep 2 && docker logs otel-door 2>&1 | grep -A4 'Data point attributes'
follow.see:
Data point attributes:
     -> model: Str(claude-opus-5-5)
     -> user.hash: Str(59355a6a057cff7f3c6201125189dd5d4a2749c7b6f0b1c3d1acf6daeda67b79)
     -> team: Str(frontend)
Value: 0.420000

lab.build: Omer, a new engineer, joins the data team on Monday, and nobody has added him to the table yet. Copy cost.json to omer.json and change the email to omer@rhinohealth.com, then send it: the record arrives with a hash but no team, so every team dashboard silently drops his cost. Fix collector.yaml in two ways. Add a statement that puts omer@rhinohealth.com in the team "data". Then add one statement, after all the people and before the hash, that sets team to "other" when no team was set (where attributes["team"] == nil), so the next person nobody added still counts somewhere. Restart the collector (docker rm -f otel-door, then the same docker run), send omer.json again, and send one more copy with an email that is in no table.
checks: A request with no token and a request with a wrong token both get 401.
A request with Bearer lab-ingest-token gets 200.
The debug output shows team: Str(frontend) and a user.hash for sean@rhinohealth.com, and no user.email anywhere.
After your change, omer.json arrives with team: Str(data), and an email that is in no table arrives with team: Str(other).
grep -c lab-ingest-token collector.yaml prints 0: the token is not in the file.

solution.text:
statements:
          - set(attributes["team"], "frontend") where attributes["user.email"] == "sean@rhinohealth.com"
          - set(attributes["team"], "backend") where attributes["user.email"] == "dana@rhinohealth.com"
          - set(attributes["team"], "data") where attributes["user.email"] == "omer@rhinohealth.com"
          - set(attributes["team"], "other") where attributes["team"] == nil
          - set(attributes["user.hash"], SHA256(Concat([attributes["user.email"], "${env:USER_SALT}"], ""))) where attributes["user.email"] != nil
          - delete_key(attributes, "user.email")

lab.fix: A teammate tidied the configuration and the collector on inf stopped starting after the deploy. Run: sed '/^  extensions: \[bearertokenauth\]/d' collector.yaml > broken.yaml && docker run --rm -e INGEST_TOKEN=x -e USER_SALT=y -v "$PWD/broken.yaml:/etc/otelcol-contrib/config.yaml" otel/opentelemetry-collector-contrib:0.161.0 2>&1 | tail -1. Read the error (it ends with 'authenticator not found'), find what the tidy removed, and explain why failing to start is better than starting without the check. Then try the other classic mistake: start the correct file without -e INGEST_TOKEN and read what the collector says.
explain: Why is it acceptable that the ingest token sits on every laptop, when we never let a GitHub token sit on an agent's VM?
The managed settings already switch prompts off. Why does the collector still delete them?
Why does the settings file for people carry no team, and where does the team come from?
lab.done: Strangers get 401, a laptop with the token gets 200, every record leaves with a team and a hash and no email, and you removed the lab with docker rm -f otel-door.

check.q: The ingest token leaks: someone pasted it into a public gist. What can a stranger do with it?

options.text: Read every team's cost numbers from the database
options.why: The token opens only the write door, on two paths. Reading goes through Grafana, which has its own login.

options.text: Write fake telemetry, until we change the token in the one place it is set
options.why: That is the whole power of this token, on purpose. The damage is junk data, and we fix it by changing the token in Vault and the admin console.

options.text: Nothing, because the WAF blocks every request that comes from outside the company
options.why: The WAF blocks attack shapes, not people outside. The address is public on purpose, so laptops off the VPN can reach it.

check.q: Why does the real ingest token go into the claude.ai admin console and not into 20-telemetry.json in git?

options.text: Because Claude Code cannot read headers from a settings file
options.why: It can: the admin console sends the same kind of settings. The question is where the secret is stored, not how it is read.

options.text: Because the admin console encrypts the telemetry on the way
options.why: HTTPS protects the data on the way in both cases. The difference is who can see the token at rest.

options.text: Because a token in git stays in every clone and in the history, even after we change it
options.why: Git never forgets. The file in git holds a fake value, and the real one lives only where it is needed.

check.q: A teammate proposes putting the team name in each person's own settings, so the collector needs no table. What goes wrong?

options.text: Each person can type any team, or none, so the team numbers depend on everyone getting it right
options.why: The same reason we scrub in the collector: a rule that depends on every laptop being right breaks on the first wrong laptop. One table in one place is correct for everyone.

options.text: Resource attributes cannot hold a team name
options.why: They can hold any name=value pair. The problem is who sets it, not whether it fits.

options.text: Nothing; it is the same result with less work
options.why: The managed settings are the same file for the whole company, so a per-person value would have to come from each person by hand, which is the problem this lesson removes.

p: The collector runs on inf-rhinohealth as a Terraform helm_release unit of the upstream OpenTelemetry Collector chart: contrib image, two replicas, a memory limiter, and an ExternalSecret that brings INGEST_TOKEN and USER_SALT from Vault (kvv2 infrastructure/otel-collector, generated by Terraform the way n8n's secrets are). The deploy reads the email-to-team table from infrastructure/ai-agents/teams and renders one set() line per person; in the Terraform template the collector's own ${env:...} is written $${env:...}, so Terraform leaves it alone. The scrub deletes prompt, prompt_text, user_system_prompt, full_command, file_path, tool_parameters and user.email. Metrics go to vminsert with Prometheus naming switched on (so the cost series is claude_code_cost_usage_USD_total), and events go to the long-term VictoriaLogs, kept for a year. There is no traces pipeline yet.

The public route otel.rhinohealth.com sits behind envoy-external with the Coraza WAF failing closed, on /v1/metrics and /v1/logs only. The people's settings live in ai-agents/settings/managed-settings.d/20-telemetry.json next to 10-models.json, with the real token pasted only into claude.ai's server-managed settings. The VM image gets a copy with no token and no OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES.

tickets.why: The collector on inf: the team table, the salted hash, the scrub, and where metrics and events are stored.
The public door: the route, the two paths, the WAF, and the bearer token checked by the collector.
The managed settings that switch telemetry on for every person and agent, content off, token only in the admin console.

words.plain: The shared key every sender puts in its Authorization header. It can only write telemetry.
The collector extension that checks the token on every request and answers 401 when it is missing or wrong.
Settings an organisation pushes to every Claude Code; a person cannot override them.
When something cannot decide or cannot start safely, it refuses instead of letting everything through.
Labels a process attaches to everything it sends, set with OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES.

review.q: Name the three places in the collector configuration that the token check needs, and what happens if one is missing.
review.a: The extension with its token (from an environment variable), the receiver's auth.authenticator, and service.extensions. Without the service entry or without the token, the collector refuses to start.

review.q: A new person joins on Monday. What must happen so her cost shows on her team's dashboard, and what does she see if nobody does it?
review.a: Someone adds her work email to the team table in Vault and the collector is deployed again. Until then her numbers arrive with a hash and team "other" (or no team at all if nobody added the fallback), never with her email.

review.q: Why does an agent's VM not get the ingest token, even though the token can only write?
review.a: The VM reads text anyone can write, so it holds no long-lived secret. It sends to a relay in the gateway with its short-lived run token, and the relay adds the ingest token.

remember: One public door, one write-only key that lives in the admin console and never in git, and one collector that turns every email into a team before anything is stored.
